introduction_markdown:
**General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. Geology 2 (0755), Paper 2, ADVANCED LEVEL, JUNE 2026. Duration: THREE HOURS.**

Instructions to candidates: Answer FOUR questions. ALL QUESTIONS CARRY EQUAL MARKS.

You are reminded of the value of clear sketches, even when not specifically demanded by the wording of the question, and of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.

questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Asteroids (2 marks).** Asteroids are **small rocky or metallic bodies (minor planets) that orbit the Sun**, most of them in the **asteroid belt between the orbits of Mars and Jupiter**. They are left-over building blocks (planetesimals) of the early Solar System that never joined together to make a planet, because of the strong gravity of Jupiter. Sizes range from a few metres to several hundred kilometres (the largest, Ceres, is about 900 to 1000 km across). Their composition is mainly silicate rock (stony), iron-nickel (metallic) or carbon-rich (carbonaceous).

**(ii) Meteors (2 marks).** A meteor is the **bright streak of light (a "shooting star" or fireball)** seen when a small solid particle from space, a **meteoroid**, enters the Earth's atmosphere at high speed and is heated by friction and compression of the air, so that it glows and usually burns up. If part of the body survives and **reaches the ground**, the recovered piece is called a **meteorite** (stony, iron or stony-iron).

**(iii) Comets (2 marks).** Comets are **small icy bodies, "dirty snowballs"**, made of frozen water, carbon dioxide, ammonia and methane mixed with dust and rock, which move round the Sun in **highly elliptical orbits** (from the Kuiper belt or the distant Oort cloud). When one nears the Sun, the ice vaporises and forms a glowing **coma** around the small solid **nucleus** and a long **tail** of gas and dust that always points **away from the Sun** because of the solar wind and radiation pressure.

The Earth is divided by its composition and by the way seismic waves travel into three main shells, with the boundaries known from seismology (the Mohorovicic discontinuity, the Gutenberg discontinuity and the Lehmann discontinuity).

**(i) The crust (4 marks)**

- **Position and thickness:** the thin outer solid shell, above the **Mohorovicic discontinuity (Moho)**. **Continental crust** is about 30 to 40 km thick on average (up to about 70 km under high mountain ranges); **oceanic crust** is only about 5 to 10 km thick.
- **Composition:** continental crust is **felsic and granitic (granodioritic) in the upper part**, rich in silica and aluminium (**sial**: Si, Al), with sedimentary rocks on top and a more mafic lower part. Oceanic crust is **mafic: basalt and gabbro** (rich in silicon, magnesium and iron, **sima**), covered by a thin layer of sediment.
- **Physical properties:** solid and brittle; average density about **2.7 g/cm³ (continental)** and about **3.0 g/cm³ (oceanic)**; P-wave velocity about 6 to 7 km/s; relatively cool (a few hundred degrees Celsius at the base); continental crust is old (up to over 4 billion years), oceanic crust is young (less than about 200 million years, because it is recycled at subduction zones).

**(ii) The mantle (4 marks)**

- **Position and thickness:** from the Moho to the **Gutenberg discontinuity** at about **2 900 km** depth; about 84 % of the volume of the Earth. It is divided into the **upper mantle** (to about 660 km, including the **asthenosphere**, a weak, partly molten zone from about 100 to 250 km, and a transition zone), and the **lower mantle** (about 660 to 2 900 km).
- **Composition:** **ultramafic rock, peridotite**, made of **olivine and pyroxene** (with garnet or spinel), rich in magnesium and iron (silicate of Mg and Fe); deeper minerals change to denser high-pressure forms (for example perovskite-type minerals in the lower mantle).
- **Physical properties:** it behaves as a **solid for seismic waves** (both P and S waves pass through, P about 8 to 13.7 km/s) but **flows very slowly (plastically)** over geological time, which makes **convection currents** that drive plate motion; temperature rises from about 1 000 °C near the top to about 3 000 to 4 000 °C at the base (approximate values); density increases from about 3.3 to about 5.5 g/cm³; the low-velocity zone of the asthenosphere has a few per cent of melt.

**(iii) The core (4 marks)**

- **Position and thickness:** from 2 900 km to the centre at about 6 370 km, with the **outer core** (about 2 900 to 5 150 km, **liquid**) and the **inner core** (about 5 150 to 6 370 km, **solid**), separated by the **Lehmann discontinuity**.
- **Composition:** mainly **iron with about 5 to 10 % nickel**, together with a few per cent of lighter elements (sulphur, oxygen, silicon, hydrogen) in the outer core. This is deduced from density, from the composition of **iron meteorites** (taken as a sample of the core of a broken planetesimal) and from seismic data.
- **Physical properties:** very dense: about **10 to 12 g/cm³** (outer core) and about **13 g/cm³** (inner core); very hot (about 4 000 to 6 000 °C, approximate) and under pressure of up to about 360 GPa; **S waves are stopped by the outer core** (so it is liquid) and P waves are slowed and refracted, creating the **P-wave shadow zone**; **convection of the liquid iron produces the Earth's magnetic field** (geodynamo); the inner core is solid because of the very high pressure, although the temperature is higher.

*Marking idea: for each layer, position, composition and physical properties, four points.*

questions.enonce_markdown:
(c) Draw and label a typical seismometer that detects vertical seismic vibrations.

(7 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Principle.** A seismometer records ground motion through **inertia**: a heavy mass is hung so that it stays almost still while the frame, fixed to the bedrock, moves with the ground; the **relative motion** between the frame and the mass is recorded. For **vertical** vibrations the mass is hung from a **spring**, so that it can move up and down.

**Diagram to be drawn (a vertical-motion seismometer).** Draw, from the top of the page downwards:

1. A rigid **support frame** (a stand with a horizontal top arm) drawn firmly attached to a **concrete pier, itself fixed to solid bedrock** (label the bedrock; the frame moves with the ground).
2. A **spring** (drawn as a coil) hanging from the top arm of the frame.
3. A **heavy mass** (inertial mass, e.g. a lead or iron block) hung from the lower end of the spring (label: "heavy mass (inertia)").
4. A **stylus (pen)** fixed to the mass, with its tip touching a sheet of paper.
5. A **recording drum** (a cylinder covered with paper, turned at constant speed by a clockwork or electric motor, with a time marker), fixed to the frame, so that the pen draws a line on it as it turns. Label the **seismogram trace** (a straight line when the ground is still; wiggles when it is shaken).
6. A **damping device** (a dashpot or a magnet with a conducting plate) attached to the mass, to stop it oscillating on after the waves have passed.
7. **Arrows** showing the vertical ground motion (up and down) and the direction of drum rotation.

(In a **modern electromagnetic seismometer** the mass carries a coil that moves in a fixed magnetic field, which produces a voltage proportional to the velocity; this signal is amplified and recorded digitally. The same labels apply: frame, spring, mass, coil, magnet, recorder.)

**How it works.** When a P wave or Rayleigh wave moves the ground up and down, the frame and drum move with it, but the heavy mass, held by the soft spring, stays almost stationary because of its inertia. The pen therefore draws the **relative motion** of the ground on the moving paper, giving a **seismogram** from which the arrival times of P, S and surface waves, and the amplitude (used for magnitude), are read.

*Marking idea: labelled frame fixed to bedrock (1), spring (1), mass (1), pen/stylus (1), drum and paper (1), damping (1), neat drawing and principle (1).*
